7568442: A visit to South Africa helped shape Kendrick Lamar’s thinking for this album. Its musical world brings together Thundercat, Flying Lotus and George Clinton, connecting Lamar’s work with jazz and funk. The people around the record offer another way into it: follow their names, and the collection begins to open into a wider musical conversation.
118630: Before it became a record, Brainfreeze was an all-45s collaboration for San Francisco’s Future Primitive parties. Cut Chemist describes the original 1999 CD as a rehearsal recording. A stack of small singles becomes a shared performance, and that performance becomes something to collect in its own right.
14457597: In Tokyo, on 17 and 18 October 1978, Directstep was recorded straight to disc. There was no overdubbing or editing between the performance and the master. That gives the record a particular kind of immediacy: the musicians had to carry the music through as it happened.
4619033: Immunity begins with a small sound from the place where it was made: Jon Hopkins’ studio door. He describes spending nine months on the album in East London. Before the music opens out, that ordinary entrance gives the record a quietly personal point of departure.
1027491: These piano studies begin with the sky. John Cage drew on star maps and the I Ching, with pianist Grete Sultan in mind. This edition contains Books I and II of Etudes Australes. It offers a meeting between a musical score, a performer and patterns found far beyond the keyboard.
8539380: Genoa and French song meet on Volume 3°. Alongside Fabrizio De André’s songwriting, the record includes adaptations of Georges Brassens and a traditional French song. Its connections cross a border through repertoire: a song can take on another voice and language while keeping a link to where it came from.
12097296: Naples is at the heart of Nuova Napoli, but Berlin is part of its making. The duo revisits the city’s disco and jazz-funk history of the 1970s and 1980s, recording at NG Tower Studios with Neapolitan collaborators. Here, the place a record evokes and the place it was recorded tell different parts of the same story.
13724942: Gary Davis describes building his Chocolate Star work in Camden with his own money, jazz training and musicians from the neighbourhood. The music brings early disco and rap into that local circle. Behind this collection is the story of someone making room for his music, and bringing the people around him into it.
14791220: Recorded at Ghana Films Studio in 1975, Ahyewa Special brings highlife together with Ahyewa rhythms. K. Frimpong and Super Complex Sounds sit at the centre of that meeting. This later licensed reissue offers a way back to a particular recording, rather than making the edition’s release country stand in for the music’s origins.
9148392: Always On grew from a week of working together in the studio. Max D joined a circle of Mood Hut musicians, including Evelyn, Jack J, Liam Butler, House of Doors and Hashman Deejay. The collaboration gives the record a human geography: a set of people sharing time and ideas in one room.
13588230: Zopelar and Benjamim Sallum began playing live improvisations together in São Paulo. This six-track EP carries connections to the Mamba Negra and ODD networks, and includes a tribute to Clube da Esquina. The record opens onto several musical circles around the duo, beyond the country attached to its edition.
8479529: The Yamaha DX100 has a place in this record’s story. The label singles it out among the classic instruments used by Gerd, while the EP sets 909 and 707 mixes alongside one another. The machinery becomes a listening invitation: compare the versions and hear how a different rhythmic frame changes the music.
